messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 3 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'SSHI_LowRipple': duplicate: same structure as an earlier design (c0001); nothing new was simulated. Values are tuned automatically, so propose a different structure.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

[c0030] SSHI_FullBridge  (topology 40eae91a637a, score 77.06, conditions passed 5/6)
D1 D pzp out DSCH
D2 D pzn out DSCH
D3 D 0 pzp DSCH
D4 D 0 pzn DSCH
L1 L pzp n1 0.00179
S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1
C1 C out 0 1.8e-06
DZ1 D 0 out DZ33
G1 SYNC ton=1.96e-05s phase=0.102 edges=both
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.37    3.38    25.2   0.157      34.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      
S2       3.28    3.31    74.2   0.188      71.6  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S3        3.4    3.41      41  0.0679      5.24  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      
S4       3.36    3.36    14.9   0.258      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      
S5       3.36    3.37      25   0.193        24  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      
S6       3.36    3.38    25.1   0.167      34.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      
failing: S2 settled: 0.07904 V (needs <= 0.02 V, margin -2.95)
S2 ripple: 0.07418 V (needs <= 0.05 V, margin -0.48)
screen (out fixed at 1.8 V): S2: 54.6 uW of 21.6 uW needed (253 %); S4: 31.7 uW of 3.24 uW needed (979 %); S6: 51 uW of 9.82 uW needed (520 %)
value sizing: 32/48 evaluations (running)

Topologies explored so far (hash: name, best score):
  2c7f143a90f6: SECE (nan)
  40eae91a637a: SSHI_FullBridge (77.06)
  b12ad9074039: SECE_DualL (nan)

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Design a piezo energy harvester interface.
    *   Requirements:
        *   `vavg` >= 1.8 V (S1-S6)
        *   `vmax` <= 3.6 V (S1-S6)
        *   `vpp` <= 0.05 V (S1-S6)
        *   `tup` <= 0.4 s (S1-S6)
        *   `dv` <= 0.02 V (S1-S6)
    *   Best design so far ([c0030] SSHI_FullBridge):
        *   Passed 5/6 conditions.
        *   S2 (heavy load: RL=150k) failed `ripple` (0.074 V > 0.05 V) and `settled` (0.079 V > 0.02 V).
        *   `vavg` is quite high (3.3V) thanks to the DZ33 zener clamp, but the ripple and stability under heavy load (S2) are the issues.
        *   The topology consists of a full bridge rectifier (D1-D4), a Zener clamp (DZ1), an L-S-SYNC (L1, S1, G1) inversion circuit, and an output capacitor (C1).

    *   S2 failing `ripple` and `settled` suggests the output capacitor `C1` is too small or the rectifier/inversion circuit isn't delivering energy smoothly enough to maintain the voltage under heavy load (150k).
    *   Wait, the values were tuned automatically. Let's look at the circuit. It's basically a full bridge with a synchronous inductor (SSHI) in parallel.
    *   The current `vavg` is near the Zener voltage (3.3V). The ripple is the peak-to-peak oscillation.
    *   The `settled` check (`dv`) compares the mean of the last 0.1s to the previous 0.1s. A failure here often means the capacitor is still charging or the system is oscillating on a slow time scale.

    *   The current design `SSHI_FullBridge` has an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ across the piezo. This is a partial SSHI.
    *   To reduce ripple and improve stability (settled), I might need a larger capacitor or a more efficient energy extraction method.
    *   However, the current structure is:
        *   Rectifier: `pzp` -> `out` (D1), `pzn` -> `out` (D2), `0` -> `pzp` (D3), `0` -> `pzn` (D4).
        *   Inductor-Switch: `pzp` -> `n1` (L1), `n1` -> `pzn` (S1).
        *   Zener: `0` -> `out` (DZ1).
        *   Cap: `out` -> `0` (C1).

    *   Wait, the inductor-switch circuit is in parallel with the piezo. When S1 closes, the energy in $C_p$ is transferred to $L_1$, and then when S1 opens, the voltage at the piezo terminals reverses, allowing more charge to flow through the rectifier. This is the essence of SSHI.

    *   To improve stability and ripple on S2 (heavy load), we might need:
        1.  A larger output capacitor (the tuner already tried this, but let's see if a different topology helps).
        2.  A more efficient rectifier (Synchronous rectification).
        3.  A different energy transfer mechanism.

    *   *Synchronous Rectification:* Replacing diodes with switches. But we only have 4 switches max and 2 SYNCs. The current design uses 1 SYNC for the inversion. We could use another SYNC for the rectification, but a full bridge needs 4 switches.
    *   *Half-bridge or charge pump:* Maybe a different arrangement.
    *   *Parallel-SSHI with a different inversion:* Maybe instead of a full bridge, use a half-bridge rectifier and a different inversion circuit? No, full bridge is generally better for piezo.

    *   Let's reconsider the L-S circuit. The current L-S circuit is `pzp` -> `L` -> `S` -> `pzn`. This is the "parallel" SSHI.
    *   Another common topology is "series" SSHI, but that requires more switches.

    *   Let's try a **Synchronous Rectifier (SR)** approach or a **Voltage Doubler/Multiplier**. But the piezo voltage is low ($\sim 3.2$ V amplitude). A bridge rectifier is appropriate.

    *   What if we use a larger capacitor? The tuner already optimized `C1` to 1.8uF. If we can't increase it more (limit 47uF), maybe the problem is the energy "packets" delivered by the SSHI.

    *   Wait, look at the `vavg` of S2: 3.28 V. The Zener is 3.3 V. It's almost clamped. The ripple is 74 mV.
    *   The `settled` failure (0.079 V) means the voltage is still drifting. With a heavy load, the capacitor charges slower.

    *   Let's try a **Synchronous SSHI** that is more integrated.
    *   Another idea: **Active Rectification**? We have 2 SYNCs. We could use one for the inversion and one for a part of the rectification.
    *   But wait, a simpler way to reduce ripple is to increase the frequency of energy delivery or the storage capacity.
    *   Maybe a **Buck-Boost** or **Charge Pump**? Too many components.

    *   Let's try a different SSHI variation. Instead of a full bridge, use a **Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI)** with a different switch configuration.
    *   Actually, the "Full Bridge SSHI" (current best) is already quite good. The failing S2 `ripple` and `settled` are the only issues.

    *   Let's look at the "settled" failure again: `dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)| = 0.079 V`. This is quite large. It means the capacitor is still charging up to the equilibrium point. This usually means the time constant $\tau = R_{eq} C_{out}$ is too large.

    *   If $R_L$ is 150k (S2), and we are delivering power, the charging current is $I_{in} - V_{out}/R_L$.
    *   To speed up startup and settlement, we need more current.
    *   The current SSHI delivers more current than a standard bridge.

    *   Let's try a **Parallel-SSHI with a different inductor placement**.
    *   Current: `L` from `pzp` to `n1`, `S` from `n1` to `pzn`.
    *   Alternative: `L` from `pzp` to `pzn`, `S` in parallel? No.
    *   Alternative: `L` from `pzp` to `out`? No.

    *   What if we try a **Synchronous Rectifier** using the second SYNC?
    *   Wait, the limit is 4 switches.
    *   Full bridge = 4 diodes.
    *   SSHI inversion = 1 switch.
    *   Total components = 4 diodes + 1 switch + 1 inductor + 1 cap + 1 zener = 8 components.
    *   We have room for more.

    *   Let's try an **Active-rectifier-like** structure using switches?
    *   If we use 2 switches for the rectifier and 2 for the inverter? No, we need 4 for a bridge.
    *   Maybe use 2 diodes and 2 switches for the bridge?
    *   Example:
        *   D1: `pzp` -> `out`
        *   D2: `pzn` -> `out`
        *   S2: `0` -> `pzp` (ctrl: G2, edges: pos)
        *   S3: `0` -> `pzn` (ctrl: G2, edges: neg)
        *   S1: `n1` -> `pzn` (ctrl: G1, edges: both)
        *   L1: `pzp` -> `n1`
        *   This uses 3 switches and 2 SYNCs.

    *   Let's rethink. The issue is the "settled" and "ripple" on S2. This is a power delivery issue.
    *   Wait, the current design `SSHI_FullBridge` is actually very close. Let's try to improve the energy extraction.
    *   Could we use a **Charge Pump**? A piezo is a current source. A bridge rectifier is basically a charge pump.

    *   Let's try **SSHI with a different inductor configuration** or a **SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)** circuit.
    *   SECE usually uses a switch and an inductor to transfer the charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ at the peaks.
    *   SECE Topology:
        *   S1: `pzp` -> `n1` (ctrl: G1, edges: both)
        *   L1: `n1` -> `out`
        *   S2: `pzn` -> `n1` (ctrl: G1, edges: both)
        *   Wait, that's not right.
        *   Correct SECE:
            *   S1: `pzp` -> `n1` (ctrl: G1, edges: pos)
            *   S2: `pzn` -> `n1` (ctrl: G1, edges: neg)
            *   L1: `n1` -> `out`
            *   This extracts charge at the peaks.

    *   Let's try the **SECE** (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction) properly.
    *   SECE Components:
        *   S1: `pzp` to `mid` (ctrl: G1, edges: pos)
        *   S2: `pzn` to `mid` (ctrl: G1, edges: neg)
        *   L1: `mid` to `out`
        *   C1: `out` to `0`
        *   DZ1: `out` to `0`
        *   Wait, this is for a different piezo model. Let's adapt.

    *   Let's try a **Double-ended SSHI** or a **modified bridge**.
    *   Actually, the simplest way to fix the "settled" and "ripple" on S2 is to increase the efficiency of the energy transfer.
    *   What if we use a **Half-Bridge Rectifier** with a center-tapped piezo? The piezo model given is just `pzp` and `pzn`. We can't center-tap it.

    *   Wait! The "S2 settled" and "S2 ripple" are the *only* failures. S2 is the heavy load.
    *   If `vavg` is 3.28V (clamped by DZ33), the ripple is 74mV.
    *   If we *remove* the Zener or *increase* its voltage, would that help? No, we must stay under 3.6V.
    *   If we *increase* the output capacitor `C1` significantly, the ripple will decrease and it will settle faster (actually, it will settle *slower* but the *ripple* will be smaller).
    *   Wait, `dv` (settled) = |mean(0.7-0.8) - mean(0.6-0.7)|. If the voltage is still rising, `dv` will be large. This means the power delivered is only slightly more than the power consumed.

    *   To fix `dv` and `ripple`, we need to deliver more power or store more energy.
    *   The `screen` says S2 delivers 54.6 uW, and 21.6 uW is needed. So there's plenty of power!
    *   Wait, if the power is enough, why is it not settling?
    *   Maybe the output capacitor is *too* large? No, the tuner chose 1.8uF.
    *   If it's not settling, it means the time constant is the problem.
    *   $V(t) = V_{final} (1 - e^{-t/\tau})$.
    *   $dv \approx V_{final} \cdot e^{-t/\tau} \cdot (1/ \tau) \cdot \Delta t$.
    *   To make $dv$ small, we need $t \gg \tau$. $\tau = C_{out} \cdot R_{eq}$.
    *   $R_{eq} = (I_{in} - I_{load}) / (V_{out} - V_{source})$.
    *   To decrease $\tau$, we need a smaller $C_{out}$ or a smaller $R_{eq}$ (more current).
    *   But if we decrease $C_{out}$, the ripple `vpp` increases!
    *   This is the classic trade-off: $vpp \approx I_{load} \cdot T / C_{out}$ and $\tau = C_{out} R_{eq}$.
    *   To satisfy both, we need to increase $I_{in}$ (the current delivered by the harvester).

    *   How to increase $I_{in}$?
        1.  Better energy extraction (SSHI/SECE).
        2.  Lower voltage drop (Synchronous rectification).

    *   Let's try **Synchronous Rectification**.
        *   Current bridge: 4 DSCH diodes. Drop $\approx 0.25$ V each $\rightarrow 0.5$ V total.
        *   If we use switches, drop $\approx 2 \Omega \cdot I$. At $10 \mu A$, that's negligible.
        *   However, we only have 4 switches.
        *   Wait, we can use a **Half-Bridge Rectifier** if we can create a virtual ground. But we can't.
        *   What if we use a **Synchronous SSHI** that also handles the rectification?
        *   Looking at the SSHI topology:
            *   D1: `pzp` -> `out`
            *   D2: `pzn` -> `out`
            *   D3: `0` -> `pzp`
            *   D4: `0` -> `pzn`
            *   L1: `pzp` -> `n1`
            *   S1: `n1` -> `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
        *   What if we replace D3 and D4 (the return diodes) with switches?
            *   S2: `0` -> `pzp` (ctrl: G2, edges: pos)
            *   S3: `0` -> `pzn` (ctrl: G2, edges: neg)
            *   This would reduce the drop from $0.25$ V to $0$ V on the return path.

    *   Let's try another topology: **The "Parallel-SSHI" with a larger inductor or different timing**. But the tuner already optimized that.

    *   What about **SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)**?
        *   SECE can be more efficient than SSHI in some cases.
        *   Structure:
            *   S1: `pzp` -> `n1` (ctrl: G1, edges: pos)
            *   S2: `pzn` -> `n1` (ctrl: G1, edges: neg)
            *   L1: `n1` -> `out`
            *   D1: `out` -> `n1` (Wait, no)
            *   Actually, a common SECE is:
                *   S1: `pzp` -> `n1` (ctrl: G1, edges: pos)
                *   S2: `pzn` -> `n1` (ctrl: G1, edges: neg)
                *   L1: `n1` -> `out`
                *   (This extracts charge at the peaks)
                *   Wait, this needs a way to prevent the inductor from discharging back. A diode `D1` from `n1` to `out`? No, `L1` is in series.
                *   Let's use the version:
                    *   S1: `pzp` -> `n1` (ctrl: G1, edges: pos)
                    *   S2: `pzn` -> `n1` (ctrl: G1, edges: neg)
                    *   L1: `n1` -> `out`
                    *   But this only works if the inductor is large enough.

    *   Wait, I have another idea. The `SSHI_FullBridge` is almost there. The only problem is the heavy load (S2).
    *   What if I use a **charge-pump** style rectifier?
        *   Piezo -> `D1` -> `C_mid` -> `D2` -> `out`
        *   This would double the voltage, but the piezo voltage is already enough.

    *   Let's try a **modified SSHI** where we use a switch to bypass the diodes? No.
    *   Let's try **SSHI with a larger output capacitor** and a **zener** that is slightly different? No, the tuner does that.

    *   Let's try a **Synchronous Rectifier + SSHI**.
        *   D1: `pzp` -> `out`
        *   D2: `pzn` -> `out`
        *   S2: `0` -> `pzp` (ctrl: G2, edges: pos)
        *   S3: `0` -> `pzn` (ctrl: G2, edges: neg)
        *   S1: `n1` -> `pzn` (ctrl: G1, edges: both)
        *   L1: `pzp` -> `n1`
        *   C1: `out` -> `0`
        *   DZ1: `out` -> `0`
        *   G1: `ton=...`, `phase=...`, `edges=both`
        *   G2: `ton=...`, `phase=...`, `edges=both` (Wait, G2 needs to close the return path).
        *   If the piezo current is $I_p \sin(\omega t)$, then when $V_{pzp}$ is positive, the current flows from `pzp` through `D1` to `out`, and returns from `0` through `S2` to `pzp`? No, that's not right.
        *   The current $I_p$ flows from `pzp` to `pzn`.
        *   If $V_{pzp} > V_{out} + 0.25$, current flows `pzp` -> `out`.
        *   To complete the circuit, it must flow from `0` to `pzn`.
        *   So:
            *   Positive cycle: `pzp` -> `D1` -> `out` -> `RL` -> `0` -> `S2` -> `pzn`.
            *   Negative cycle: `pzn` -> `D2` -> `out` -> `RL` -> `0` -> `S3` -> `pzp`.
            *   S2 closes when $V_{pzp}$ is positive (current flows `0` to `pzn`).
            *   S3 closes when $V_{pzp}$ is negative (current flows `0` to `pzp`).

    *   Let's refine this "Hybrid Synchronous Bridge":
        *   D1: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
        *   D2: `pzn`, `out` (DSCH)
        *   S2: `0`, `pzp` (ctrl: G2)
        *   S3: `0`, `pzn` (ctrl: G2)
        *   S1: `n1`, `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
        *   L1: `pzp`, `n1`
        *   C1: `out`, `0`
        *   DZ1: `0`, `out` (DZ33)
        *   G1: `ton=...`, `phase=...`, `edges=both`
        *   G2: `ton=...`, `phase=...`, `edges=both`
        *   Wait, S2 and S3 are controlled by the same G2. G2 can't do both "pos" and "neg" with different switches.
        *   We need two SYNCs for the return path? No, we only have 2 SYNCs total.
        *   G1 for inversion, G2 for return path.
        *   If G2 is `edges=both`, it closes S2 and S3 at the same time. That's a short circuit!
        *   We must use different SYNCs or different edges.
